pains.title: The practice, the ASC and the owners blur together
pains.problem: The practice bills the professional fee, the ASC bills the facility fee, and owners hold different shares of each. Partners argue about money nobody can reconcile.
pains.how: Lucid reports each entity and ASC fee splits separately, reconciles shared staff and management fees, and gives you one combined owner view.

pains.title: Implant and supply costs hide the margin on each case
pains.problem: Some payers pay implants separately and others fold them into the case rate, so a busy surgical week can still lose money.
pains.how: Lucid reports margin per procedure net of implants and supplies, by surgeon, with payer mix next to it.

pains.title: Cash tied up in slow payers and injury cases
pains.problem: Workers compensation and letter of protection cases pay late, and one missed authorization can hold up a surgery.
pains.how: Your biller still works the cases. Lucid's cash forecast shows your bank balance and expected cash together, so a shortfall shows up before payroll.

faq.q: How should an orthopedic practice keep the books when we own part of an ASC?
faq.a: The practice and the ASC should each have their own books and P&L, because they bill different fees and often have different owners. Lucid reports ASC and facility fee splits apart from the professional fee, reconciles what the entities share and gives you a combined owner view.

faq.q: How do I know if my orthopedic cases make money after implant costs?
faq.a: You need cost and revenue tied to each procedure type, not only a monthly total. Lucid reports margin per procedure net of implants and supplies, by surgeon too, so you see which procedures and which surgeons earn a margin and which ones lose it.

faq.q: How should we account for personal injury and letter of protection cases that take a year or more to pay?
faq.a: Track them apart from insurance receivables, age them by case and keep a reserve for what you usually collect. Lucid's CFO planning can model your cash forecast with that money left out until it arrives.

faq.q: Why does my orthopedic practice run short on cash when we are busy?
faq.a: The work is done up front and the money arrives weeks or months later, especially from workers compensation and injury cases. Lucid's cash flow reporting and forecasting platform shows your expected cash next to your bank balance, so you can plan payroll and credit lines around a shortfall.

faq.q: How do I know if my in house imaging, physical therapy or DME is profitable?
faq.a: Each service line needs its own revenue and its own staff, equipment and space costs. Lucid sets up profit by service line and shows monthly results for each one, with CFO modelling when you want to test an ancillary.
